content.text: I have everything needed. SCOPe 2.08 places all three groups as distinct families under one superfamily, which fixes the strength of the inference.

answers.answer:
SCOPe placement (current release 2.08, frozen 2021-07-28). All three groups are classified in class d (alpha+beta), fold d.144 'Protein kinase-like (PK-like)' (sunid 56111), and in the single superfamily d.144.1 'Protein kinase-like (PK-like)' (sunid 56112). Within that superfamily they are SEPARATE families: canonical protein kinases = d.144.1.7 'Protein kinases, catalytic subunit' (sunid 88854); aminoglycoside phosphotransferases = d.144.1.6 'APH phosphotransferases' (sunid 64411; e.g. APH(3')-IIIa, APH(3')-IIa/kanamycin kinase); PI3Ks = d.144.1.4 'Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), catalytic domain' (sunid 56171; e.g. d4ps3a4 from 4ps3). Other families in the same superfamily (actin-fragmin kinase d.144.1.3, TRP Ca-channel kinase domain d.144.1.5, Rio2 C-terminal kinase domain d.144.1.9) show how broad the superfamily is.

What is justified. (1) Homology: SCOPe's superfamily level asserts probable common ancestry based on shared structure and function despite low sequence identity. So protein kinases, APHs and PI3Ks are best regarded as divergent homologs sharing a common ancestral phosphotransferase scaffold, not convergent look-alikes. (2) Shared mechanism: the conserved bilobal architecture (small N-lobe with a beta-sheet and the alpha-C-like helix; larger mostly alpha-helical C-lobe), ATP bound in the inter-lobe cleft, and the conserved catalytic machinery (Lys/Glu pair positioning the ATP phosphates, catalytic-loop Asp as base, metal-binding Asp of the DFG/DxG-like motif, Mg2+-coordinated gamma-phosphate transfer) are shared, so an in-line direct phosphoryl-transfer mechanism to a hydroxyl acceptor is a reasonable common inference. (3) ATP-site chemistry: ATP-competitive inhibitor binding modes are partly shared, which is why some protein-kinase inhibitors bind APHs and PI3Ks and vice versa (e.g. wortmannin/LY294002 and kinase inhibitors cross-reacting; PI3K-related kinases mTOR/ATM/DNA-PK are sequence-related to the PI3K family).

What is NOT justified. Superfamily membership says nothing reliable about the ACCEPTOR substrate: these families phosphorylate chemically different acceptors (protein Ser/Thr/Tyr hydroxyls; aminoglycoside sugar hydroxyls; inositol-ring 3-OH of phosphoinositide lipids). Because they are in different families (< ~30% identity, family-level boundary), substrate specificity, substrate-recognition loops/surfaces, oligomeric state and regulatory mechanisms cannot be transferred. Protein-kinase regulation (activation-loop phosphorylation, alpha-C helix in/out and DFG in/out switching, pseudosubstrate inhibition, regulatory-subunit or SH2/SH3-domain control, scaffolding) is largely absent in APHs (constitutively active bacterial resistance enzymes with a short acceptor-binding region) and differs in PI3Ks (regulation by p85 adaptor/nSH2-iSH2 contacts, Ras binding, helical and C2 domains, membrane recruitment; the PI3K ABD is a separate superfamily d.15.15 in SCOPe). Even within the protein-kinase family, Ser/Thr vs Tyr specificity and consensus motifs vary and are not predictable from fold alone; pseudokinases in the same family have lost catalysis entirely. Fold-level similarity (d.144) carries even less: SCOPe fold membership alone would not justify any functional transfer, and SCOPe is a structure classification of representative PDB entries, not a functional annotation; family and species representatives are not exhaustive, and 'automated matches' entries (e.g. sunid 190091 under d.144.1.7) are assigned by sequence similarity to classified domains without manual curation.

Evidence required before transferring substrate specificity or regulation. (a) Sequence-level evidence within the family: high identity to a characterized member, conservation of catalytic residues (VAIK Lys, alpha-C Glu, HRD catalytic Asp, DFG Asp, APE/activation-loop motifs or their APH/PI3K equivalents), and conservation of the substrate-recognition residues (e.g. the Tyr- vs Ser/Thr-kinase determinants in the catalytic loop and P+1 loop; the APH acceptor-site residues; the PI3K activation-loop residues that determine PI(4,5)P2 vs PI selectivity). (b) Structural evidence: a co-crystal or cryo-EM structure with the substrate/acceptor or a substrate analog, not just an apo or ATP-bound structure; comparison of the substrate-binding groove and activation-segment conformation; positional conservation of the metal-binding and catalytic Asp residues. (c) Direct biochemical evidence: in vitro kinase or phosphotransferase assays showing phosphorylation of the proposed acceptor (peptide/protein, aminoglycoside, or lipid) with kinetic parameters (kcat/KM) and site mapping by mass spectrometry; for lipids, assays with defined lipid substrates on membranes. (d) Regulation evidence: demonstration of the regulatory mechanism itself (activation-loop phosphorylation state, dependence on regulatory subunits or Ca2+/calmodulin, cyclin, or adaptor binding; autoinhibition by domain deletion/mutation), using mutagenesis of the proposed regulatory residues and cellular/genetic data (knockouts, phosphoproteomics). (e) Phylogenetic placement: a tree of the kinase-like superfamily (e.g. ePK vs ELK/atypical kinases) to confirm the query falls within the family, and domain-architecture analysis (accessory domains such as PH, SH2, C2, helical, Ras-binding) which largely determine localization and regulation. (f) Inhibitor profiling or chemical proteomics if a pharmacological inference (shared ATP-site ligands) is to be made. Without (a)-(d), only the generic conclusions—shared ATP-binding fold, Mg-dependent phosphoryl transfer, broadly similar catalytic residues—should be transferred across these three families.

(c) Direct biochemical evidence: in vitro kinase or phosphotransferase assays showing phosphorylation of the proposed acceptor (peptide/protein, aminoglycoside, or lipid) with kinetic parameters (kcat/KM) and site mapping by mass spectrometry; for lipids, assays with defined lipid substrates on membranes. (d) Regulation evidence: demonstration of the regulatory mechanism itself (activation-loop phosphorylation state, dependence on regulatory subunits or Ca2+/calmodulin, cyclin, or adaptor binding; autoinhibition by domain deletion/mutation), using mutagenesis of the proposed regulatory residues and cellular/genetic data (knockouts, phosphoproteomics). (e) Phylogenetic placement: a tree of the kinase-like superfamily (e.g. ePK vs ELK/atypical kinases) to confirm the query falls within the family, and domain-architecture analysis (accessory domains such as PH, SH2, C2, helical, Ras-binding) which largely determine localization and regulation. (f) Inhibitor profiling or chemical proteomics if a pharmacological inference (shared ATP-site ligands) is to be made. Without (a)-(d), only the generic conclusions—shared ATP-binding fold, Mg-dependent phosphoryl transfer, broadly similar catalytic residues—should be transferred across these three families.
